claims.claim: Modernity has traditionally been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment through a process of de-naturalization, but Hannah Arendt questioned this conviction.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modernity, in philosophical and sociological literature, has “traditionally” been presented as the age when artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment. The process of modernization, from this point of view, is the process of de-naturalization . This widely shared conviction has ba - sically been questioned by Hannah Arendt.

definitions.definition: The process where artifacts supplant nature and destroy the originally given natural environment.
A process taking place during the centuries of the modern age to the detriment of the commonly created and uphold human world, enhanced by technology.

distinctions.distinction: The Arendtian critique of modernity takes a difference between the notions of Earth and world.

must_not_be_lost: Arendt's view that modernity is an age of world-alienation and re-naturalization rather than simply de-naturalization.
extraction.segment_function: Introduction, intellectual context, and paper hypothesis concerning Hannah Arendt's interpretation of the natural and the artificial in The Human Condition.
unresolved_context: The full implications of how Heidegger's philosophy influenced Arendt's distinction between Earth and world within the broader text.

claims.claim: Arendt's political ontology in The Human Condition is based on a phenomenological approach rooted in German Existenz-philosophy.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The political ontology explained in the book was based on a phenomenological approach rooted in the German Existenz -philosophy.

claims.claim: The search for an extraterrestrial Archimedean point involves a radical modification of the human condition.
claims.supporting_excerpt:
The search for an ex -
traterrestrial Archimedean point, Arendt argues, involves a radical modification of
human condition so far having been determined by the circumstances of our native
planet

definitions.definition: A human being on the existential level who is imprisoned in the endless repetitive cycles of consumption and production, consuming natural goods or producing things for biological maintenance without creating lasting entities.

distinctions.distinction: The human artifice separates human existence from all mere animal environment, whereas life itself remains outside this artificial world, through which man remains related to all other living organisms.

must_not_be_lost: Arendt's view on the alteration of the human condition caused by space technology and satellite launch.
The definition of the earth as the quintessence of the human condition providing a unique habitat.
extraction.segment_function: introduction and ontological definition of Arendt's theory regarding the human condition, space technology, and the relation between the natural and artificial
unresolved_context: Margaret Canovan's questioning of The Human Condition as Arendt's opus magnum.

claims.claim: Labor is described as a mere animal activity in Arendt's ontology, wherein humanity is considered the most dangerous of animal races.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Labor , summarizing this train of thought, is a mere animal activity in the ontology of Arendt.

claims.claim: Action is identified as the highest and most specifically human activity, taking place in the world of things created by homo faber.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The third and highest stage of human existence, in the ontology of Arendt, is the level of action taking place in the world of things created by homo faber . Action is the most specifically human activity; to act and to be free is the same, Arendt concludes.

definitions.definition: A mere animal activity conditioned by life and situated in the private realm for the satisfaction of biological needs.
A tool-making and tool-using agent capable of creating lasting and durable things, constituting the human world and the terrain of human artifice.
The third and highest stage of human existence, which constitutes human plurality and is unimaginable without speech.

distinctions.distinction: The private realm is the terrain of life-sustaining labor and where homo faber works, whereas the public realm is the domain of action enriched by the fruits of work.
Necessity stands as a synonym for the social, while liberty stands as a synonym for the political.

must_not_be_lost: The triad of labor, work, and action embeds the antithetical notion-pairs of necessity-liberty and social-political.
extraction.segment_function: Examines the triad of human activities (labor, work, and action) in Arendt's ontology and their connection to the natural and artificial realms.

claims.claim: Process is the antithesis of action, functioning as a sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law that creates a terrain of necessity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Process is the antithesis of action which needs free, undetermined human individuals being able to initiate new beginnings in the world. Process is the sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law regulating the order of these changes. The ensuing events of a process are links in a cause–effect chain where the later states of temporal development are casually determined by the former ones. The realm of processes is a terrain of necessity.

claims.claim: Modernity in its first phase is characterized by the victory of homo faber using means-end rationality to produce artificial things, with fabrication inherently entailing violence against nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modernity, at least in its first phase, for her, means the victory of homo faber who, under the guidance of means-end rationality , began, in ever-increasing amount and speed, to produce large variety of artificial things. Homo faber seemed to become the master of the Earth who continuously expands the reach of his power over his environment. The activity of fabrication inherently entails the element of violence directed against lifeless and living nature.

definitions.definition: The sequence of changes predetermined by an inner impersonal law regulating their order, serving as the antithesis of action and embodying the realm of necessity.

distinctions.distinction: Process is a sequence of changes predetermined by impersonal law and necessity, whereas action requires free, undetermined human individuals able to initiate new beginnings.
Process involves fluidity, ephemerality, and futility, standing in opposition to the durability, endurance, and lastingness of the man-created artificial world.

must_not_be_lost: The association of the social with the natural and the political with the artificial.
The characterization of process as a metaphor covering the negative side of modernity and endangering the spatial economy of human existence.
references_to_other_sections: It is the chapter IV of the book (Arendt 1958: 79–175)

claims.claim: Fabrication inevitably involves an over-all reification of nature and acts as a destroyer of nature through an element of violation and violence.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This element of violation and violence is present in all fabrication and homo faber , the creator of human artifice, has always been a destroyer of nature.

claims.claim: In the second phase of modernity, animal laborans rises to dominance and technological productivity paradoxically annihilates the lasting artificial world by flooding it with natural processes.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The second phase of modernity entails the victorious rise of animal laborans who embodies the natural part of human being ensuring the futile, perishable goods of consumption needed for the mere biological survival of humanity as one among other animal spe - cies. The thing-character of the artificial world created by the irresistibly expanding technology is melting away in an ever growing speed. Natural processes are flooding the lasting artificial constructions of human existence.

definitions.definition: The creator of human artifice who objectifies everything, conducts himself as lord and master of the whole Earth, and whose productivity involves the destruction of nature to erect a man-made world.
The embodiment of the natural part of human beings that ensures futile, perishable goods of consumption needed for mere biological survival.

distinctions.distinction: Animal laborans remains the servant of nature and the Earth ensuring biological survival through consumption, whereas homo faber conducts himself as lord and master of the whole Earth through fabrication and destruction of nature.

extraction.segment_function: To analyze Hannah Arendt's interpretation of homo faber, fabrication, and the shift from the artificial-technological sphere to the dominance of animal laborans in modernity.

claims.claim: Arendt asserts that the rationality required for constructing machines and launching artificial processes is an animal rather than a human ability, functioning as a modified animal instinct to maintain biological existence.
claims.supporting_excerpt:
Arendt puts forward an astonishing and strange assertion: rationality needed for construction of machines and getting involved in launching artificial processes, an sich , for her, is an animal and not human ability. Rationality, in her argumentation, a special modified kind of animal instinct, whose function is to find the necessary means to reach the shared end of all living organ -
isms; the maintenance of their biological existence

claims.claim: Modern technology does not build a lasting artificial human world, but instead serves to fulfill consumption needs and ensure the continuous functioning of human metabolism with nature.
claims.supporting_excerpt:
The emerging gigantic machine of human technology does not contribute to the upkeep of the lasting artificial human world; it serves to fulfill the needs of consumption, in other words, it ensures, in an ever-expanding cycles, the un -
disturbed functioning of the processes of human metabolism with nature.

definitions.definition: The application of rationality to create a common human world which is our lasting and durable home and a dwelling place for human plurality.
A condition of modernity described by Arendt where the technological world is a pseudo-artifact and modern humanity is reduced to a 'world-poor' animal race bound by biological necessity.

distinctions.distinction: Animal laborans engages in labor subject to the everlasting cycles of human metabolism with nature, whereas homo faber creates products and a durable common world that do not fall prey to these cycles.

must_not_be_lost: Arendt's view that modern technology serves biological necessity rather than durability.
The characterization of modernity as an age of re-naturalization.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze Arendt's conception of modernity, distinguishing between animal laborans and homo faber, and arguing that modern technology serves biological necessity and re-naturalization rather than building a durable human world.

must_not_be_lost: The connection between The Origins of Totalitarianism and The Human Condition regarding re-naturalization processes.

claims.claim: In her closing chapter, Arendt returns to the narrative of cultural criticism where re-naturalization and the fading out of action embody the main threat of modernity rather than environmental pollution.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is re-naturalization, for her, and not human construed artifice which embodies the main threat of modernity. She more fears for the fading out of action from the world than the pollution of the environment.

must_not_be_lost: The problem of the relation for artificial and natural has been fit into a double narrative in The Human Condition
